## This week’s sociological question

<div class="chapter-question">When a model predicts an unobserved answer or study result, what exactly has been recovered?</div>

## Connection to the preceding material

Week 7 asked what a synthetic response represents. Week 8 moves to a narrower prediction task: begin with real human data, hide some of it and ask a model to predict what was not observed. This makes validation possible, but only if we specify whether the target is a person’s answer, a population distribution, a group difference, an election result or a relationship among variables.

## Learning outcomes

You should be able to distinguish imputation, retrodiction and prediction of never-asked opinions; separate individual accuracy from aggregate resemblance; explain why a plausible record can still distort a population; trace the first `for` loop one case at a time; and compare hosted and local model results without treating either route as the truth.

## Essential readings and what each contributes

::: {.reading-list}
- **Methods:** Kim and Lee (2026), “AI-Augmented Surveys.” Read the complete paper. It uses observed survey answers to predict unasked items for real respondents and distinguishes augmentation from wholesale replacement. [Preprint](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.09620). [@KimLee2026]
- **Methods and validation:** Xie et al. (2026), “Evaluating the Statistical Realism of LLM-Generated Social Science Data.” Read the complete article. It asks whether success on a selected statistic survives broader tests of joint distributions and relationships among variables. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.2538145123). [@XieEtAl2026]
- **Substantive application:** Lax and Phillips (2009), “Gay Rights in the States,” *American Political Science Review* 103(3): 367–386. Read the complete article. It applies multilevel regression and poststratification to state opinion and asks whether policy responds to public preferences on gay rights. This is an established comparison for claims about recovering quantities we did not directly observe. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1017/S0003055409990050). [@LaxPhillips2009]
:::

## Sociological and methodological background

The 2016 election is a useful warning against treating polls and forecasts as the same thing. National polls were accurate by historical standards and correctly showed Hillary Clinton winning the popular vote. State polls had larger errors and called the wrong winner in Pennsylvania, Michigan and Wisconsin, which together changed the Electoral College outcome.

The AAPOR post-election committee found the strongest evidence for two causes. First, many state surveys contained too many college graduates and did not weight by education. Education was strongly related to presidential vote in these states, so this pushed estimates toward Clinton. Second, substantial numbers of voters decided during the final week and broke heavily for Trump after much of the state polling had finished. The committee found no general evidence for a “shy Trump” effect. Turnout changes may have contributed, but tests of likely-voter models produced small and inconsistent effects.

Forecasting models introduced another layer of uncertainty. They combined state polls with assumptions about how polling errors move across states and how much opinion could still change. Their estimates of Clinton’s probability of winning ranged from 71 percent to more than 99 percent. The committee agreed that polls and forecasts answer different questions, although its members did not reach a single verdict about election forecasting. The practical lesson is to inspect both the survey inputs and the assumptions used to turn those inputs into probabilities.

Election forecasting belongs to a much broader history of efforts to put social systems inside computers. The World3 model linked population, food, industrial output, pollution and resources through feedback loops. Sugarscape populated a landscape with artificial agents whose local rules generated inequality, migration, trade and conflict. The 2006 Sentient World Simulation proposal went further still, describing a continuously updated “synthetic mirror” of the world for testing possible courses of action. These projects are interesting precisely because they model different objects and validate them in different ways.

This is no longer only an academic exercise. Simile now sells simulated populations for testing how the same audience might respond to different messages, concepts and prices. Artificial Societies markets linked networks of personas for surveys, focus groups, experiments and longer scenario cascades. These descriptions come from the companies themselves and should be read as product claims. In academic work, AgentSociety places LLM agents in linked urban, social and economic environments and reports simulations of 30,000 agents. The technical scale is striking, but the central social-scientific question remains whether the system reproduces the relevant human behavior in a new setting.

These cases concern different targets. A poll estimates current reported opinion. An election forecast estimates a later outcome. A simulation estimates how people might respond to an intervention. Small-area estimation addresses another problem again: how to estimate opinion in a place where the direct sample is thin. Lax and Phillips combine actual survey responses, a multilevel model and census population counts to estimate state opinion, then use those estimates to study policy responsiveness. Their evidence chain matters because observed answers and known population margins constrain the estimate, and the estimates can be compared with direct surveys and election data.

An LLM prediction changes this chain. Kim and Lee train on questions, respondents’ other answers and survey years to study three tasks: imputing a missing answer, retrodicting an item not asked in a particular wave and predicting an opinion never asked in the survey. These tasks expose the model to different amounts of relevant evidence and therefore warrant different claims.

## Synthesis of the current LLM literature

Xie and colleagues evaluate whether generated datasets preserve distributions, bivariate associations, multivariate relationships, life-event sequences and links between sequences and covariates. Their results show why “the synthetic data look realistic” is too vague. A model can approximate a marginal distribution while compressing subgroup variation or changing relationships among variables. Kim and Lee likewise separate individual- and aggregate-level performance and compare their retrodictions with surveys in the Roper archive. They also raise a further question: whether researchers should infer an opinion that a respondent did not disclose.

Ashokkumar and colleagues evaluate a different target: treatment effects. They compare model-predicted and observed effects across 70 nationally representative survey experiments. The predictions rank effects well, but systematically overstate their size. Centaur asks a related question at a different level. It is fine-tuned on trial-by-trial choices from 160 cognitive experiments and tested on unfamiliar participants, cover stories, task structures and domains. Neither result licenses the claim that a language model is generally “human-like.” Each is evidence about specified tasks and comparisons.

The coding example adopts the Ashokkumar comparison in a deliberately simpler form. Three published experiments provide different contexts: voter turnout, hotel towel reuse and risky choice. OpenRouter and Ollama predict the control and treatment rates from the study description; only then are the published human rates revealed. The loop preserves every raw return and calculates the treatment-effect error for each model and context. The slides and Python page include one dated local-model result for the towel experiment so that we can inspect a real overestimate before running the full exercise. This is a teaching benchmark rather than a reproduction of Ashokkumar et al., who simulated demographically diverse participants and aggregated their responses.

## Summary and preparation for next week

A model can be evaluated against answers it did not see, but the result is always relative to a stated target. Week 9 changes the unit of analysis: the model supplies advice inside a labour process. The first student-edited function makes that workplace configuration explicit.
